title: Conditions and Validation
subtitle: Conditions and Validation: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on conditions and validation, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Conditions and Validation: foundations and mental model

Conditions and Validation is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Conditions select paths using Boolean expressions. Test below, at, and above boundaries, and make overlapping branches deliberate. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A course portal must validate requests and keep generated output and database interactions safe. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Conditions and Validation: Chooses a message from the score threshold
blocks.code:
$score = 82;
if ($score >= 80) { echo "Strong progress"; } else { echo "Keep practising"; }
blocks.output: Chooses a message from the score threshold.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “$score = 82;”: Assigns or updates state; later lines observe the new value, so the right-hand expression matters. Line 2 — “if ($score >= 80) { echo "Strong progress"; } else { echo "Keep practising"; }”: Checks a condition or selects a branch; the result determines which path executes. Expected behavior: Chooses a message from the score threshold. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A lesson should unlock at exactly 100 XP. Which threshold is correct?
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: xp >= 100. Greater-than-or-equal includes the boundary value 100.
blocks.reasoning: Greater-than-or-equal includes the boundary value 100. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Conditions and Validation: Trims and normalizes input before strict comparison
blocks.output: Trims and normalizes input before strict comparison.

blocks.text: Example 2 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “$answer = strtoupper(trim(" b "));”: Assigns or updates state; later lines observe the new value, so the right-hand expression matters. Line 2 — “if ($answer === "B") { echo "Correct"; }”: Checks a condition or selects a branch; the result determines which path executes. Expected behavior: Trims and normalizes input before strict comparison. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A submitted answer may include surrounding spaces and lowercase letters. What should happen before comparison?
options: Compare the raw text and reject every lowercase answer
Convert the answer to a number without checking it
Accept any non-empty string as correct
Trim whitespace and normalize case, then compare with an accepted option
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Trim whitespace and normalize case, then compare with an accepted option. Normalization removes irrelevant format variation while the actual answer still must match.
blocks.reasoning: Normalization removes irrelevant format variation while the actual answer still must match. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Conditions and Validation: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Conditions select paths using Boolean expressions. Test below, at, and above boundaries, and make overlapping branches deliberate. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A course portal must validate requests and keep generated output and database interactions safe. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Conditions and Validation: Rejects whitespace-only values

blocks.text: Example 3 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “$name = "   ";”: Assigns or updates state; later lines observe the new value, so the right-hand expression matters. Line 2 — “if (trim($name) === "") { echo "Name required"; }”: Checks a condition or selects a branch; the result determines which path executes. Expected behavior: Rejects whitespace-only values. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A value can be missing, zero, or positive. Why should those cases not automatically share one branch?
options: Conditions cannot distinguish these states
The display color determines the numeric value
They may have different meanings and need explicit handling
All programming languages treat missing as zero
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: They may have different meanings and need explicit handling. Absence and numeric zero are different states unless the domain explicitly defines them as equivalent.
blocks.reasoning: Absence and numeric zero are different states unless the domain explicitly defines them as equivalent. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Conditions and Validation: A match expression maps distinct states to labels in PHP 8 and later
blocks.output: A match expression maps distinct states to labels in PHP 8 and later.

blocks.text: Example 4 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “$status = "ready";”: Assigns or updates state; later lines observe the new value, so the right-hand expression matters. Line 2 — “$label = match ($status) { "locked" => "Locked", "ready" => "Ready", "complete" => "Complete", default => "Unknown" };”: Defines an expression, mapping, or function result; the left side supplies the input and the right side determines the behavior. Expected behavior: A match expression maps distinct states to labels in PHP 8 and later. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A status can be locked, available, or complete. What makes the logic easier to audit?
options: Convert all statuses to true
Handle each valid status and define a deliberate fallback for unknown input
Use nested conditions with no final else/default
Assume downloaded statuses always match expected values
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Handle each valid status and define a deliberate fallback for unknown input. Explicit states and a fallback make the behavior for invalid or newly added states visible.
blocks.reasoning: Explicit states and a fallback make the behavior for invalid or newly added states visible. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Conditions and Validation: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Conditions select paths using Boolean expressions. Test below, at, and above boundaries, and make overlapping branches deliberate. For the Code Academy dashboard, A course portal must validate requests and keep generated output and database interactions safe. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses conditions and validation. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A condition uses `score > 80`, but the specification says scores of 80 or above qualify. What is the defect?
options: The boundary score 80 is excluded
Every value above 80 is excluded
The comparison always returns a string
The condition becomes a loop
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: The boundary score 80 is excluded. The comparison operator does not match the wording of the requirement.
blocks.reasoning: The comparison operator does not match the wording of the requirement. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Conditions select paths using Boolean expressions. Test below, at, and above boundaries, and make overlapping branches deliberate. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
